output.title: When rollback drills are worth the time
output.body:
If you run a small business, the cost of a rollback drill is usually not a software problem. It is the time it takes to write down how you would undo a broken workflow before money, orders, or customer data get stuck.

That makes it a simple owner decision: do the drill when the cost of a bad day is higher than the time you spend preparing for one. If the workflow handles payments, customer records, or other repeatable steps, the question gets more important. Human approval still has to stay in place for money movement.

A useful check is this: if the workflow breaks on a Friday afternoon, can you restore it quickly, or would you spend the rest of the day untangling it by hand? If you do not know, you probably need a rollback drill.

The practical next step is to map the current manual fallback, or at least identify the single point of failure that would stop the workflow. That gives you the starting point for a drill, without pretending the automation is safer than it is.

Rollback drills are unglamorous. They are only worth the time when the cost of failure is bigger than the cost of being ready for it.
